title: Por Ahora: the Llanero, the Barracks on the Hill, and the Bolivarian Republic
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Llanos, the Barracks, the Tree

stops.name: Sabaneta, the three-room house of Rosa Inés
stops.date_confidence: attested; the birth date is fixed in every biography and in the 2014 heritage decree on the house
stops.campa: In a three-room house of palm and mud on Calle 10, in a llanos town of dirt streets, Elena Frías gives birth to her second son. Barinas in the 1950s is cattle country and floodplain, and the federal wars are still inside family memory. The house belongs to his paternal grandmother, Rosa Inés Chávez, and it is she who raises him: his parents are village schoolteachers with seven children coming and no room for all of them. He calls her mother for the rest of his life, and works beside her in the street selling papaya sweets off a tray.
suggested_refs: The birth house, no. 85 between calles 10 and 11, Sabaneta, declared a Cultural Asset of the Nation in March 2014
sources: Marcano and Barrera Tyszka, Hugo Chávez: The Definitive Biography

stops.name: Barinas, the Liceo O'Leary and the pitcher's arm
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the secondary years in Barinas city are attested in the biographies, the exact campus and the exact years are not independently confirmed, and the month and day are placeholders
stops.campa: He is sent from the town to the state capital for secondary school and boards there, a country boy in a provincial city. He pitches, seriously and well, and means to make the major leagues; he says later that he entered the military academy in large part because the academy was in Caracas and the scouts were in Caracas. The arm never carries him to a mound in the United States. The family house in Barinas is still standing, and in July 2022 the government orders it converted into a second museum of him.
suggested_refs: The Chávez family house in Barinas city, ordered converted to a museum in July 2022
sources: Marcano and Barrera Tyszka, Hugo Chávez: The Definitive Biography
El Nacional, 'Jorge Arreaza anuncia que la casa familiar de Hugo Chávez se convertirá en un museo' (July 2022)

stops.name: Caracas, the Academia Militar at Fuerte Tiuna
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of entry (1971) and the year of commissioning (1975); month and day are placeholders
stops.campa: At seventeen he enters the military academy on the Avenida Los Próceres, a llanero among the sons of the capital, in the first cohorts of a reformed curriculum that gives cadets political science and history alongside drill and the rifle. He reads Simón Bolívar, Simón Rodríguez the tutor, and Ezequiel Zamora the federal general of the llanos, and takes the three of them as one doctrine. He graduates in 1975 as a second lieutenant, reported eighth in his class. His first posting is counterinsurgency in the eastern mountains, against the remnant of the Venezuelan guerrilla.
suggested_refs: The Plan Andrés Bello curriculum of the Venezuelan military academy, which gave the promotions of the 1970s a university-style political formation
sources: New York Review of Books summary of Marcano and Barrera Tyszka
Academia Militar de Venezuela institutional history

stops.name: Maracay, the red berets of the paratroop garrison
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the Aragua paratroop postings are attested in unit histories but the sequence and dates of individual assignments are not established, and the date here orders the segment only
stops.campa: Posted to the parachute troops garrisoned at Maracay, he jumps with the men who will still be standing beside him in February 1992. Barracks life in Aragua is close and talkative. Officers of the same promotion drink together and complain about the parties in Caracas and the money leaving the country; the complaint is general in the garrison, and nothing above them acts on it. Here he takes the red beret of the paratroop arm, and he is still wearing it as a civilian twenty years later.
suggested_refs: The 42nd Paratroop Infantry Brigade at Maracay, the unit culture from which the 1992 conspiracy was drawn
sources: 42.a Brigada de Infantería Paracaidista institutional history

stops.name: Samán de Güere, the oath under the tree
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the date is fixed in Chavista commemoration and the cell certainly existed, but the ceremony under the tree rests on later participant recollection, and at least one Venezuelan commentator places the oath instead in the officers' casino of the Cuartel Páez at Maracay
stops.campa: On the road between Maracay and Turmero stands a samán already a national monument since 1933, said to have sheltered Bolívar's troops. Beneath it, on the anniversary of Bolívar's death, four officers swear an oath: Chávez, Jesús Urdaneta Hernández, Felipe Acosta Carles, Raúl Baduel. They take the words Bolívar swore on the Monte Sacro in Rome and adapt them, promising not to rest until the chains that oppress the people are broken. They name the cell EBR-200, the Bolivarian Revolutionary Army, for the bicentenary of the Liberator's birth. It becomes MBR-200 only later.
suggested_refs: The Samán de Güere, Parroquia Samán de Güere, Municipio Mariño, Aragua, site of the annual 17 December commemoration
sources: Fundación Comandante Eterno Hugo Chávez, 'Realiza el juramento bajo el Samán de Güere'
PSUV, 'Juramento ante el Samán de Güere'
Reeditor.com opinion column disputing the location

stops.name: Caracas, the 23 de Enero: the Caracazo
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Carlos Andrés Pérez, elected on the memory of the oil boom he presided over in the 1970s, announces an austerity package agreed with the International Monetary Fund. Bus fares rise, and on the twenty-seventh of February the country comes down off the hills. Looting spreads from Guarenas into Caracas and outward across the republic. The army is sent into the barrios above Miraflores and fires into them for days. The official dead are counted in the hundreds and the unofficial in thousands; mass graves at La Peste are opened years afterwards.
suggested_refs: The common graves of La Peste in the Cementerio del Sur, exhumed in the 1990s
sources: Corrales and Penfold, Dragon in the Tropics

stops.name: Caracas, the Cuartel de la Montaña: the fourth of February
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: From the hilltop barracks above the 23 de Enero, which looks straight down on the presidential palace, Lieutenant Colonel Chávez directs the rising. Units move that night in Caracas, Maracay, Valencia, and Maracaibo. In the interior the conspirators take their objectives and hold them. In the capital they do not: Pérez gets out of the airport, reaches a television station, and speaks to the country before the rebels can. By morning the operation consists of a man on a hill with a radio, and nothing coming back over it.
suggested_refs: The Cuartel de la Montaña, Monte Piedad, 23 de Enero, command post of the 4 February 1992 rising
sources: Accounts of the February 1992 Venezuelan coup attempt

stops.name: Caracas, Miraflores: the palace that does not fall
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The seat of government is the whole point of the operation, and the seat of government holds. Rebel armour reaches the gates and cannot force them; the president is not inside to be taken. Fighting across the city kills soldiers and civilians both, the totals differing according to who compiles them. Chávez orders the units in the capital to stop, and offers his surrender on a single condition: that he be permitted to say so himself, on television, in uniform, so that the men still fighting elsewhere will believe it is his voice.
suggested_refs: The Palacio de Miraflores, objective of the 4 February assault and Chávez's seat for the following fourteen years
sources: PBS Frontline/World coverage of the 1992 rebellion

stops.name: Caracas, Fuerte Tiuna: two minutes of television
stops.date_confidence: attested that the message was recorded after his surrender at the Ministry of Defence in Fuerte Tiuna and then broadcast nationally; some accounts place the recording in a channel studio, which appears to confuse it with the rebels' assault on the state broadcaster that morning
stops.campa: Taken to the Ministry of Defence at Fuerte Tiuna, he is put in front of a camera in uniform and given under two minutes. He does not plead and does not blame. He tells the rebels still holding out in Aragua and Valencia to lay down their arms, states that the objectives were not achieved in the capital, and assumes personal responsibility for the movement. Two words in the middle of that sentence carry everything that comes after: por ahora, for now. The tape goes out nationally. He goes to prison.
stops.quote: Compañeros: Lamentablemente, por ahora, los objetivos que nos planteamos no fueron logrados en la ciudad capital.
stops.quote_source: Televised surrender broadcast, 4 February 1992; full transcript reproduced at Rebelión, PSUV.org.ve, and Qué Pasa, 'Seis discursos para entender el 4-F'
suggested_refs: The full text of the 4 February 1992 broadcast, including the appeal to the units still holding out: 'Oigan al comandante Chávez, quien les lanza este mensaje para que, por favor, reflexionen y depongan las armas'
sources: Rebelión transcript of the 4 February 1992 broadcast
Not Even Past, 'Por Ahora: The Legacy of Hugo Chávez Frías'

stops.name: San Francisco de Yare, the cell that becomes a salon
stops.date_confidence: period, February 1992 to March 1994; the year is given to order the segment and the month and day are placeholders
stops.campa: Two years in the penitentiary at Yare, in the valleys of the Tuy. He reads and he receives: intellectuals, priests, retired guerrillas, party men who want to see for themselves what he is. The cell becomes an office. In November 1992 a second uprising by officers of his movement fails while he is locked up and commanding nobody. The argument about what he means is carried on outside, by other people, for the whole two years. He writes Cómo salir del laberinto at Yare.
suggested_refs: Cómo salir del laberinto, written at Yare
sources: Council on Foreign Relations, 'Venezuela's Chavez Era' timeline

stops.name: San Francisco de Yare, the charges dismissed
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by the Venezuelan presidential event archive, PSUV, and Analítica; older summaries give only the year 1994
stops.campa: Rafael Caldera, who founded COPEI and then won the presidency against it, had risen in the Congress on the night of the coup to say that no people could be asked to immolate itself for a democracy that could not feed it. Now, three months into his second term, he grants a sobreseimiento to Chávez and fourteen other officers and non-commissioned officers held at Yare. The charges are dropped on one condition: Chávez must request his own retirement from the armed forces. He walks out on the twenty-sixth of March, a civilian.
suggested_refs: Caldera's speech to the Venezuelan Congress of 4 February 1992, the political opening that made the 1994 dismissal possible

stops.name: Havana, the Aula Magna: received as a head of state
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Nine months out of prison, holding no office and leading no party, he lands in Havana on the fourteenth of December 1994 and finds Fidel Castro waiting at the foot of the aircraft steps with honours reserved for heads of state. Cuba is deep in the período especial, the Soviet subsidy gone and the lights out for hours a day. Castro takes him to the great hall of the university, introduces him, and gives him the podium. Chávez speaks of Bolívar and of a Venezuela twenty years off.
suggested_refs: The Aula Magna of the University of Havana, where Chávez spoke on 14 December 1994
sources: CIPI, Centro de Investigaciones de Política Internacional
Max Azicri on the Castro-Chávez alliance

stops.name: Caracas, the vote that ends the Punto Fijo
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Standing for the Movimiento Quinta República against the whole architecture of the Punto Fijo pact, Chávez takes 56.20 percent and 3,673,685 votes against Henrique Salas Römer's 39.97. Acción Democrática and COPEI, which had passed the presidency between them for forty years, withdraw their own candidates in the last days to prop up Salas, and it makes no difference. Carter Center observers report a peaceful and credible vote. The pact was signed in 1958. It ends on the sixth of December 1998.
suggested_refs: Carter Center observation reporting on the 1998 Venezuelan presidential election

stops.name: Caracas, the moribund constitution
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the inauguration and the substance of the oath; the exact wording circulates in Venezuelan secondary reproductions rather than in a primary gazette or audiovisual transcript verified here
stops.campa: He swears the presidential oath on the constitution of 1961 and calls it, with his hand on it, moribund: a dying charter over which he promises to drive the transformations that will give the new republic a magna carta fit for new times. The formula has no legal weight, and everyone in the chamber understands it exactly. Within two months a referendum authorises a constituent assembly. The assembly elected in July is his by a margin that leaves the opposition six seats out of a hundred and thirty-one.
stops.quote: Juro delante de Dios, juro delante de la Patria, juro delante de mi pueblo que sobre esta moribunda Constitución impulsaré las transformaciones democráticas necesarias para que la República nueva tenga una Carta Magna adecuada a los nuevos tiempos. Lo juro.
stops.quote_source: Presidential inaugural oath, 2 February 1999, Caracas; widely reproduced in the Venezuelan press, not verified here against a primary transcript
suggested_refs: The April 1999 referendum authorising the Constituent Assembly
sources: ConstitutionNet summary of Venezuela's 1999 constituent process

stops.name: Caracas, the Bolivarian Republic named
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The new constitution is approved by 71.8 percent of votes cast on a turnout near 44 percent. The referendum is held while the Vargas landslides are burying the coast. The country is renamed the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela. The two chambers of Congress become one National Assembly, the presidential term runs six years with one immediate reelection allowed, and the state assumes a long schedule of social rights it now owes its citizens by law. Chávez carries a pocket blue copy of the text everywhere and reads from it on television.
suggested_refs: The Constitution of the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, 1999, and the pocket blue edition distributed in the millions

stops.name: Caracas, the Teatro Teresa Carreño: OPEC comes back
stops.date_confidence: attested; the summit ran 26 to 28 September 2000 and opened on the twenty-sixth, which some summaries give incorrectly as the twenty-seventh
stops.campa: Reelected in July under his own constitution, beating Francisco Arias Cárdenas, one of the officers who rose with him in 1992, Chávez opens the second summit of OPEC heads of state and government. It is the first such meeting since Algiers in 1975 and he presides over it. His argument to the producers is old and simple: the cartel is worth nothing unless its members hold their quotas together, and Venezuela, which spent the 1990s quietly overproducing, is now the member saying so. It closes on the twenty-eighth with the Declaration of Caracas.
suggested_refs: The Declaration of Caracas, 28 September 2000, closing document of the Second OPEC Summit
sources: Carter Center reporting on the July 2000 election

stops.name: Caracas, Miraflores: doctors for crude
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the thirtieth of October 2000 Castro comes to Caracas and the two sign the Comprehensive Cooperation Convention. Venezuela will ship oil to Cuba on preferential terms and long credit; Cuba will send physicians, teachers, sports trainers, and technical personnel. It is a barter between a country with crude and no doctor resident in its slums and a country with trained doctors and no fuel. Within three years thousands of Cuban physicians are living in Venezuelan barrios, in rooms above the consultorios.
suggested_refs: The Cuba-Venezuela Comprehensive Cooperation Convention, 30 October 2000
sources: Max Azicri on the Castro-Chávez alliance

stops.name: Caracas, the forty-nine laws
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month of November 2001; the day is a placeholder
stops.campa: Under an enabling law the government promulgates forty-nine decrees in a single package, without sending any of them through the National Assembly. A hydrocarbons law raises the state's royalty and requires majority state ownership in new ventures. A land law permits the expropriation of idle estates. A fisheries law favours the small boats over the industrial trawlers. Fedecámaras, the union confederation CTV, the church hierarchy, and the private broadcasters find themselves on the same side within the same season. Not one of the decrees is withdrawn.
suggested_refs: The 2001 Ley Orgánica de Hidrocarburos and the Ley de Tierras, the two decrees that consolidated the opposition
sources: Human Rights Watch reporting on the period
Corrales and Penfold, Dragon in the Tropics

stops.name: Caracas, Fuerte Tiuna: the letter not signed
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: A general strike becomes a march on Miraflores, and the march ends in gunfire around the Puente Llaguno. Nineteen die, government supporters and opposition marchers both, and the question of who fired first is never settled to anybody's satisfaction. That night the high command demands his resignation and takes him into custody at Fuerte Tiuna. He refuses to sign the letter they put in front of him. By morning Pedro Carmona Estanga has been proclaimed president and has dissolved the Assembly, the courts, and the constitution.
suggested_refs: The Carmona decree of 12 April 2002, dissolving every elected body in the republic
sources: OAS report on the April 2002 rupture
Carter Center characterisation of the episode as a temporary coup

stops.name: Isla La Orchila, the island they fly him to
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He is flown out to the naval installation on La Orchila, a low island in the Caribbean well off the coast, to keep him away from any garrison that might still obey him. He asks for a priest. He writes a note stating that he has not resigned and has not abandoned the office; it is carried off the island and read on air. On the mainland the barrios come down the hills a second time, for him now, and the paratroop garrisons of Maracay declare against Carmona.
suggested_refs: Chávez's handwritten note from La Orchila, 13 April 2002: 'No he renunciado al poder legítimo que el pueblo me dio'
sources: Contemporary reporting on the April 2002 coup

stops.name: Caracas, Miraflores: back before dawn
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Carmona's government lasts about forty-eight hours. It dissolves every elected body in the country in its first decree and loses the army before the second day is out. A helicopter brings Chávez back from La Orchila in the dark, before dawn on the fourteenth, and he walks into Miraflores holding a small crucifix, into a crowd that has been outside all night. He speaks for hours and asks for calm. In the weeks that follow the officers who moved against him are retired one by one.
suggested_refs: The July 2002 U.S. State Department Office of Inspector General review, which found no evidence of State Department participation in the coup while documenting American funding of opposition-linked civil society groups
sources: OAS report on the April 2002 rupture
Congressional Research Service summary of the State Department OIG report

stops.name: Caracas, PDVSA La Campiña: the strike and the firings
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the start of the strike on 2 December 2002 and the 31 January 2003 dismissal figure
stops.campa: Opposition parties, Fedecámaras, the CTV, and most of the technical and managerial staff of the state oil company shut the industry down from the second of December. Production collapses; tankers sit at anchor with striking captains aboard; a country made of petroleum queues for petrol. The government calls it sabotage and the strikers call it a strike to force an early election. It breaks after two months without forcing one. By the thirty-first of January some five thousand three hundred employees have been dismissed, and thousands more follow.
suggested_refs: Petróleos de Venezuela after the 2002-2003 paro, rebuilt around executive-loyal personnel
sources: Reuters contemporary reporting, December 2002 and 31 January 2003
IMF documentation of PDVSA's post-strike role

stops.name: Caracas, Catia: the Cuban doctors move in
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 2003 for the launch of Barrio Adentro; the specific inaugural clinic is approximate to the programme's known Caracas origin and the month and day are placeholders
stops.campa: The first consultorios open in the hillside barrios of western Caracas: two rooms, a Cuban doctor living upstairs, free consultations in neighbourhoods where no physician had been resident within memory. The programme is called Barrio Adentro, inside the barrio. Others follow it, funded straight out of oil revenue and run outside the ministries: literacy, subsidised food, adult secondary schooling, cataract surgery. The Lancet reports on the results. Critics report that the parallel structure leaves the ordinary hospital system to rot.
suggested_refs: The Misión Barrio Adentro network of consultorios populares and its Cuban medical staffing
sources: The Lancet reporting on Barrio Adentro

stops.name: Caracas, the recall survived
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The opposition gathers signatures, the electoral council disputes them, the signatures are gathered a second time, and the recall referendum is finally held in August. Chávez wins it with roughly 59 percent against 41. The Carter Center and the OAS audit the machines and endorse the count. The opposition rejects the result, and the following year boycotts the National Assembly elections, handing him a legislature with no opposition in it whatsoever. Oil that year is above forty dollars a barrel and rising.
suggested_refs: The Carter Center final audit report on the 2004 presidential recall referendum

stops.name: Havana, the Palacio de la Revolución: ALBA signed
stops.date_confidence: attested; the coordinate is the Palacio de la Revolución on the south side of the Plaza de la Revolución, corrected from a value about 1.4 km south of the building
stops.campa: Ten years to the day since Castro met him at the aircraft steps, the two sign in Havana the declaration founding the Bolivarian Alternative for the Americas. It is written explicitly against the Free Trade Area of the Americas that Washington has been proposing since 1994: not tariff schedules but barter, cooperation agreements, subsidised oil, doctors counted as payment. It begins with two members. Bolivia, Nicaragua, Ecuador, and a string of Caribbean states join later. At Mar del Plata in November 2005 the FTAA negotiation collapses.
suggested_refs: The founding declaration of ALBA, Havana, 14 December 2004

stops.name: Caracas, Aló Presidente 249: Mr. Danger
stops.date_confidence: attested to the broadcast of 19 March 2006; Aló Presidente travelled the country, so the Caracas pin is the canonical city coordinate rather than a verified studio location
stops.campa: On the two hundred and forty-ninth edition of Aló Presidente, the Sunday programme that runs without a script and sometimes for eight hours, Chávez addresses George W. Bush directly by the nickname he has given him: Mr. Danger, borrowed from the North American in Rómulo Gallegos's Doña Bárbara, the man who comes to the llanos to take the land. He calls him a coward, a genocidaire, a drunkard, and an ignoramus, and then says it in English for the benefit of the addressee. Venezuelan crude keeps arriving at United States refineries on schedule throughout.
stops.quote: You are a donkey, Mr. Danger.
stops.quote_source: Aló Presidente No. 249, 19 March 2006, in Chávez's own English rendering of the line
suggested_refs: Rómulo Gallegos, Doña Bárbara (1929), source of the Mister Danger figure
sources: PSUV.org.ve, 'En 2006 Chávez a Bush: ¡Eres un donkey, Mr. Danger!'

stops.name: New York, the United Nations: the rostrum still smells
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He walks to the rostrum of the General Assembly the morning after George W. Bush has spoken from the same place, crosses himself, holds up a book by Noam Chomsky, and tells the hall that the Devil was here yesterday and that the podium still smells of sulphur. The speech runs well past its allotted time. Some delegates laugh and some walk out. The line is on every front page in the hemisphere by morning, and Venezuela, campaigning that autumn for a seat on the Security Council, does not get it.
stops.quote: The Devil came here yesterday, right here. It still smells of sulphur today.
stops.quote_source: Address to the United Nations General Assembly, 20 September 2006; English text as published on Wikisource
suggested_refs: The full 20 September 2006 UN address, including 'I have the feeling, dear world dictator, that you are going to live the rest of your days as a nightmare because the rest of us are standing up'
sources: Wikisource, 'Address to the United Nations General Assembly (Chávez, 2006-09-20)'
george_w_bush.journey.json, stop 'United Nations Headquarters, the smell of sulphur'

stops.name: The Orinoco Belt, the majority taken
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Fresh from 62.84 percent against Manuel Rosales, the largest majority of his career, Chávez comes to the heavy-oil fields of the Faja on the first of May and raises the flag over the upgraders. The four Orinoco projects pass to joint ventures in which the state holds at least sixty percent. Chevron, BP, Total, and Statoil accept minority terms and stay. ExxonMobil and ConocoPhillips refuse and leave for international arbitration, where the argument outlives him by years. The telephone company and the electricity company are bought back the same year.
suggested_refs: The 2007 Orinoco Belt migration to mixed companies under the 2001 hydrocarbons law
sources: Carter Center reporting on the December 2006 election

stops.name: Caracas, the concession not renewed
stops.date_confidence: attested to May 2007; the day given is the night the terrestrial signal was replaced
stops.campa: The government declines to renew the terrestrial broadcasting concession of Radio Caracas Televisión, on air since 1953 and open in its support for the coup of April 2002. At midnight the signal is replaced by a new state channel. Students who have never marched before fill the avenues of eastern Caracas for weeks afterwards. The government's case is that a public spectrum licence is the state's to grant and the state's to withhold. Human Rights Watch calls it the heaviest single blow to media pluralism in the country's democratic era. RCTV continues on cable for three more years.
suggested_refs: Human Rights Watch reporting on the 2007 RCTV concession decision
sources: Contemporary reporting on the RCTV closure

stops.name: Santiago de Chile, the summit and the king
stops.date_confidence: attested that the exchange occurred at the Ibero-American Summit in Santiago in November 2007 and that Al Jazeera reported the quoted line on 12 November; the day given is the day of the closing session and is not independently confirmed here
stops.campa: At the Ibero-American Summit he interrupts the Spanish prime minister to call the previous prime minister, José María Aznar, a fascist, on the ground that Aznar's government recognised the Carmona administration within hours in April 2002. King Juan Carlos leans into his microphone and asks him why he does not shut up. The question becomes a mobile phone ringtone in Spain within days. Given the floor again, Chávez does not withdraw the word, and explains what he takes it to mean.
stops.quote: Fascists are not human. A snake is more human.
stops.quote_source: Chávez at the Ibero-American Summit, Santiago de Chile, November 2007, quoted by Al Jazeera, 'Chavez hits back at Spanish king', 12 November 2007
suggested_refs: The 2007 Ibero-American Summit at Santiago and the '¿por qué no te callas?' exchange
sources: Contemporary Spanish and Latin American press

stops.name: Caracas, the reform refused
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The proposed constitutional reform runs to sixty-nine articles: indefinite reelection, a six-hour working day, new forms of communal property, wider emergency powers. It is put to the country in two blocks and both are voted down, narrowly, on a heavy abstention among his own supporters. It is the only national vote he loses in fourteen years. He goes before the cameras within hours of the count, accepts the announced result, and tells the winners their victory is worth nothing.
suggested_refs: Carter Center reporting on the December 2007 constitutional referendum

stops.name: Caracas, the term limits removed
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Fourteen months after the defeat he puts a single amendment to the country instead of a package of sixty-nine: the removal of term limits from every elected office, mayors and governors and the presidency alike. Framed that way it passes. Article 230 now permits a president to stand as often as he can win an election. His supporters call this democracy and his opponents call it a man arranging his own permanence. He is fifty-four, and speaks of governing until 2021.
suggested_refs: Article 230 of the Venezuelan constitution as amended in February 2009

stops.name: Caracas, the Panteón Nacional: the sarcophagus opened
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Shortly after midnight, filmed for the country, the sarcophagus of Simón Bolívar is opened in the National Pantheon. Chávez has persuaded himself that the Liberator did not die of tuberculosis at Santa Marta in 1830 but was killed by his Colombian enemies, and he wants the bones examined. He watches the work and afterwards writes that he has seen the glorious skeleton, that Bolívar lives, that he wept. The forensic commission finds no evidence of poisoning. An attempt to confirm the remains by DNA fails for want of a maternal relative.
suggested_refs: The 2010 exhumation of Bolívar's remains and the report of the forensic commission

stops.name: Havana, CIMEQ: the first tumour
stops.date_confidence: the public announcement of 30 June 2011 is attested; the surgery date is approximated from that announcement and is not independently confirmed
stops.campa: He had gone to Havana in June for what was announced as a pelvic abscess. At the Centro de Investigaciones Médico Quirúrgicas the Cuban surgeons remove a cancerous tumour instead. On the thirtieth he appears on Cuban television in a tracksuit, gaunt, beside a photograph of Fidel Castro, and tells Venezuela what has happened. Chemotherapy begins in July, in Havana rather than Caracas. In October he declares himself free of cancer. No organ of origin is named, in that announcement or in any that follow.
suggested_refs: The Centro de Investigaciones Médico Quirúrgicas, Siboney, Havana, where all four operations were performed
sources: Contemporary press coverage of the 30 June 2011 announcement

stops.name: Havana, CIMEQ: the same region again
stops.date_confidence: attested to 26 February 2012, corrected from summaries giving 28 February; he announced the new lesion on 21 February and radiation began after his return to Cuba on 24 March
stops.campa: He announces on the twenty-first that a new lesion has appeared in the same region and flies to Havana. The tumour, about two centimetres, is removed on the twenty-sixth. He goes back a month later for radiation therapy and spends the spring travelling between the treatment and a country he intends to campaign in. His own constitution requires the president to be present in order to govern, and the National Assembly votes him permission for each absence.
suggested_refs: The National Assembly authorisations for presidential absence, 2011-2013
sources: La Nación and El Colombiano cancer chronologies

stops.name: Caracas, the fourth election
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He campaigns from the roof of a truck in the rain, swollen from steroids, no longer able to walk the distances he once walked, and closes in Caracas before a crowd that fills the avenues on the fourth of October. The new term is to begin on the tenth of January. On the seventh he takes about 55 percent against Henrique Capriles Radonski, the narrowest margin of his four presidential wins and still eleven points. The Carter Center calls the vote peaceful in a bitterly polarised campaign.
suggested_refs: Carter Center reporting on the October 2012 Venezuelan presidential election

stops.name: Caracas, Miraflores: the name of the successor
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He appears on television flanked by the entire leadership of the movement and says that the cancer has returned a third time, that he must go back to Havana to be operated on, and that if anything should happen that disqualifies him, the country should elect Nicolás Maduro. He has never named a successor before. For fourteen years he has been the movement in his own person, and the movement has no other name to put on a ballot. He flies to Havana within days.
suggested_refs: The televised address of 8 December 2012, the only public act of designation Chávez ever made
sources: Bloomberg, 'Chavez Names Loyalist Heir as Venezuela Eyes Succession', 9 December 2012

stops.name: Havana, CIMEQ: the fourth operation
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The fourth operation runs for hours. What follows is delivered to the country in communiqués: a severe respiratory infection, then insufficiency, then a tracheal tube and a cannula through which he cannot speak. He does not come home for the inauguration of the tenth of January. The Supreme Tribunal rules that the swearing-in may be deferred, since a reelected president continues in office without interruption, and the government stays in place around an absent man. Photographs published in February show him lying down with a copy of Granma.
suggested_refs: The Supreme Tribunal ruling of 9 January 2013 on administrative continuity
sources: Congressional Research Service report on Chávez's death

stops.name: Maiquetía, home in the dark
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He is flown into Maiquetía in the small hours of the eighteenth of February, after two months and more out of the country, and driven up to the military hospital in Caracas without being seen by the crowds who have waited along the road for him. Motorcycle columns of supporters follow the ambulance up the autopista. The government reports that treatment continues and that he is governing in writing. He is fifty-eight. Nobody outside the hospital and the family sees him alive again.
suggested_refs: The Aeropuerto Internacional Simón Bolívar at Maiquetía, point of his last return
sources: Reuters and RFE/RL coverage of the February 2013 return

stops.name: Caracas, the Hospital Militar: twenty-five past four
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He dies at the Hospital Militar Dr. Carlos Arvelo on the afternoon of the fifth of March, at twenty-five minutes past four. Maduro announces it on television with the high command behind him, hours after expelling two United States military attachés from the country. The government never publishes the histopathology, and the absence of a diagnosis feeds a decade of claims that the disease was given to him. The commander of his honour guard tells the Associated Press that at the end Chávez could not speak and shaped the words with his lips.
stops.quote: I don't want to die. Please don't let me die.
stops.quote_source: Reported words of Chávez, as recounted by General José Ornella, head of the presidential honour guard, to the Associated Press, 7 March 2013; a single secondhand account of a private, unrecorded moment
suggested_refs: The Hospital Militar Dr. Carlos Arvelo, San Martín, Caracas
sources: Associated Press via Fox News, 'Hugo Chavez's last words'

stops.name: Caracas, the Academia Militar: lying in state
stops.date_confidence: attested; the body lay at the academy from 6 March, the state funeral was held on 8 March, and the remains stayed there until 15 March
stops.campa: The coffin is carried from the hospital to the military academy where he was a cadet, a route of a few kilometres that takes seven hours because the crowd will not open. He lies in state under the vaulted hall for nine days. The queue runs for kilometres and people sleep in it overnight. Thirty-two heads of state attend the funeral on the eighth. In Havana, Fidel Castro writes a Reflexión saying that on the fifth of March, in the afternoon hours, died the best friend the Cuban people ever had.
stops.quote_source: Fidel Castro, 'Reflexiones' column, Granma, March 2013, English translation reproduced in MercoPress, 12 March 2013
suggested_refs: Castro's Granma Reflexión on Chávez's death, closing on Che Guevara's formula
sources: MercoPress, 'Chávez, the best friend of the Cuban people in their history, says Fidel Castro', 12 March 2013

stops.name: Caracas, the Cuartel de la Montaña: back up the hill
stops.date_confidence: attested to 15 March 2013, corrected from summaries dating the interment to July 2013
stops.campa: The plan to embalm him and display him like Lenin is abandoned. A pathologist advises that preservation had to begin within about eight hours of death; a Russian commission estimates seven or eight months of work, in Russia. The body has had three formaldehyde treatments for the wake and that is all it will have. On the fifteenth of March it is carried up to the Cuartel de la Montaña, the barracks he commanded the rising from in 1992, and laid in a sarcophagus by the architect Fruto Vivas. A cannon fires there every afternoon at twenty-five past four.
suggested_refs: The Mausoleo Flor de los Cuatro Elementos at the Cuartel de la Montaña 4F, inaugurated 15 March 2013
sources: Infobae, 'Confirmaron que no será embalsamado el cuerpo de Hugo Chávez', 15 March 2013
Reuters, 'Chavez shrine draws crowds of pilgrims a month after his death'

stops.name: La Guaira, the statues come down
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: After the presidential election of the twenty-eighth of July, in which the electoral council declares Maduro the winner without publishing the tally sheets, protests break out across twenty of the twenty-three states. Crowds pull down statues of Chávez in at least five of them. Statues of him had been attacked in 2017 and in 2019, never on this scale. In La Guaira a twelve-foot figure that Maduro himself dedicated in 2017 is hauled off its plinth, dragged behind motorcycles, doused in petrol, and set alight.
suggested_refs: The July 2024 statue-toppling wave, recorded across roughly 187 demonstrations in 20 of 23 states
sources: Infobae, 'Videos: así fueron derribadas las estatuas de Hugo Chávez', 30 July 2024
Fox News coverage of the toppling

stops.name: Caracas, the mausoleum reported struck
stops.date_confidence: attested that the claim circulated and that fact-checkers disputed it; the underlying military operation and its consequences are recent and still contested in the reporting
stops.campa: During the United States military operation in Caracas that ends with Maduro's capture, video circulates showing the hill of the 23 de Enero under fire, captioned as the destruction of the mausoleum. Venezuelan outlets carry it. Chequeado, EFE Verifica, and Newtral find no evidence that the building was hit: satellite imagery and local broadcasts afterwards show the structure standing, and the authorities report no damage in that sector. The footage is dated to other places. The sarcophagus is where it was.
suggested_refs: Chequeado, 'Es falso que este video muestra un ataque al mausoleo de Chávez'
